result.topic_en: Euler notes that the third Euler-type equation $M\partial x = \partial S$ is implied by the other two, then begins Problem I: finding the space curve that maximizes or minimizes $\int \frac{x\,\partial y\,\partial z}{\partial x}$, deriving $qx=a$ and $px=b$.
result.transcription:
24
oriretur ista aequatio: $M\partial x = \partial S$, quae ergo cum binis prae-
cedentibus $N\partial x = \partial P$ et $N'\partial x = \partial P'$ commode conjungi
poterit. Interim tamen probe est observandum, quamlibet
harum trium aequationum jam in binis reliquis esse conten-
tam, ideoque omitti posse, nisi insignem usum in calculo
evolvendo saepissime praestaret. His notatis istud argu-
mentum prorsus novum aliquot exemplis illustremus.
Problema I.
Investigare lineam curvam ternis coordinatis x, y et z
contentam, in qua haec formula integralis: $\int \frac{x\partial y\partial z}{\partial x}$ ma-
ximum minimumve obtineat valorem.
Solutio.
12. Cum igitur sit $\partial y = p\partial x$ et $\partial z = p'\partial x$, cujus
loco commoditatis gratia scribamus $\partial z = q\partial x$, quandoqui-
dem haec littera $q$ in primo significatu hic non amplius
occurrit, formula nostra integralis erit $\int pqx\partial x$, ita ut sit
$V = pqx$, hincque differentiando $\partial V = pq\partial x + px\partial p + px\partial q$,
unde facta collatione habebimus $M = pq$; $N = 0$; $N' = 0$;
$P = qx$; et $P' = px$, hincque fiet $S = -pqx$, quamobrem
tres nostrae aequationes erunt:
$1^{\circ}.\ pq\partial x = -\partial.pqx$; $2^{\circ}.\ 0 = \partial.qx$ et $3^{\circ}.\ 0 = \partial.px$.
13. Ex binis posterioribus aequationibus fit $qx = a$
et $px = b$, unde tota quaestio jam sponte resolvitur. Cum

items.english: Any one of these three equations is already contained in the other two, and can therefore be omitted.

items.english: To find the curve described by three coordinates x, y and z, for which the integral formula $\int \frac{x\,dy\,dz}{dx}$ attains a maximum or minimum value.
